title: Holly Hunter
wiki_lead:
Holly Hunter (born March 20, 1958) is an American actress. Born in Conyers, Georgia, her first acting role was as Helen Keller in a fifth-grade play, before appearing in Rockdale County High School stagings of Oklahoma!, Man of La Mancha, and Fiddler on the Roof. In Pittsburgh, she graduated with a drama degree at Carnegie Mellon University and performed in local theater. 
Hunter then moved to New York City with Frances McDormand, beginning a Broadway career. After appearing in a slasher film released in 1981, The Burning, she moved to Los Angeles a year later, taking on various supporting roles in theatrical and television films, before starring in Raising Arizona (1987) and receiving the Berlin Film Festival's Silver Bear and her first nomination at the Academy Awards for her starring role in Broadcast News (1987).  She later went on to win two Primetime Emmy Awards for Outstanding Lead Actress for her performances in the television films Roe vs. Wade (1989) and The Positively True Adventures of the Alleged Texas Cheerleader-Murdering Mom (1993).
Hunter won the Academy Award for Best Actress for her performance as a mute Scottish woman in The Piano (1993). That same year, she was also nominated for the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for the legal thriller The Firm (1993). She earned another Oscar nomination in the same category a decade later for the coming-of-age drama Thirteen (2003). Other major accolades she has won include an AACTA Award, a BAFTA Award, a Cannes Film Festival Award, and a Golden Globe.

Early life
Hunter was born in Conyers, Georgia to Marguerite "Dee Dee" (née Catledge), a homemaker, and Charles Edwin Hunter, a part-time sporting goods company representative and farmer with a 250-acre farm. She is the youngest of six children. Her parents encouraged her talent at an early age, and her first acting part was as Helen Keller in a fifth-grade play. She is unable to hear with her left ear due to a childhood case of the mumps. The condition sometimes leads to complications at work, and some movie scenes have to be altered from the script for her to use her right ear. She is irreligious. She began acting at Rockdale County High School in the early 1970s, performing in local productions of Oklahoma!, Man of La Mancha, and Fiddler on the Roof. Hunter earned a degree in drama from Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh and for a while performed in local theater, playing ingenue roles at City Theater, then named the City Players.


Career

Hunter moved to New York City and roomed with fellow actress Frances McDormand, living in the Bronx "at the end of the D (subway) train, just off 205th Street, on Bainbridge Avenue and Hull Avenue". A chance encounter with playwright Beth Henley, when the two were trapped alone in an elevator, led to Hunter's being cast in Henley's plays Crimes of the Heart (succeeding Mary Beth Hurt on Broadway), and Off-Broadway's The Miss Firecracker Contest. grok_lead: Holly Hunter (born March 20, 1958) is an American actress celebrated for her intense and versatile portrayals across film and television, earning her the Academy Award for Best Actress for her role as the mute pianist Ada McGrath in the drama The Piano (1993). Her career spans decades, with breakthrough performances in the Coen brothers ' comedy Raising Arizona (1987), where she played the determined Edwina "Ed" Cutwater, and James L. Brooks ' Broadcast News (1987), earning her first Oscar nomination for Best Actress as ambitious TV producer Jane Craig. Hunter has also voiced the superheroine Helen Parr/Elastigirl in Pixar's The Incredibles franchise (2004â2018), starred as flawed cop Grace Hanadarko in the TNT series Saving Grace (2007â2010), which garnered her two Primetime Emmy nominations, and portrayed corporate executive Rhea Jarrell in HBO's Succession (2018â2023). In 2025, she starred as Madeline Vance in the Netflix film The Electric State, and in 2026, she will lead as Chancellor Nahla Ake in the Paramount+ series Star Trek: Starfleet Academy. Born in Conyers, Georgia, as the youngest of seven children to homemaker Opal Marguerite Catledge and sporting goods dealer Charles Edwin Hunter, Hunter grew up on a family poultry farm that instilled in her a strong work ethic. She became deaf in her left ear due to a childhood infection but pursued her passion for performing, participating in high school theater before attending Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, where she earned a Bachelor of Fine Arts in drama in 1980. After graduation, Hunter relocated to New York City, sharing an apartment with aspiring playwright Frances McDormand and filmmaker Joel Coen, which led to early collaborations on stage and screen. Hunter's professional debut came with a small role in the horror film The Burning (1981), followed by supporting parts in Swing Shift (1984) and the Coens' neo-noir Blood Simple (1984). Her star rose in the late 1980s with lead roles in Raising Arizona and Broadcast News, the latter showcasing her rapid-fire delivery and emotional depth, solidifying her as a leading talent in independent and mainstream cinema. The 1990s brought further acclaim, including an Oscar-nominated turn in The Firm (1993) as a resilient wife, alongside Emmy wins for television movies Roe vs. Wade (1989) and The Positively True Adventures of the Alleged Texas Cheerleader-Murdering Mom (1993). Transitioning to television in the 2000s, Saving Grace marked her first series lead, blending dark humor with spiritual themes and earning her Golden Globe and Screen Actors Guild nominations. Hunter's later career reflects her commitment to complex characters, from the mother in Thirteen (2003) to the media mogul in Succession, while her voice work in The Incredibles highlighted her range in animation.
